entities.name: Spanish House of Habsburg
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Spanish House of Habsburg (the Spanish Habsburgs, r. 1516-1700), established when Charles I of Spain (Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor) inherited the Spanish Crown from his maternal grandparents Ferdinand and Isabella, ruled Spain at the height of its global power — governing the largest empire in world history at its peak (16th-17th centuries), encompassing Spain, the Americas from Mexico to Argentina, the Philippines, Portugal (1580-1640), the Netherlands, Naples, Sicily, and Milan. The 'Spanish Century' under Philip II was history's first truly global empire, with trade connections linking every inhabited continent.

Philip II (r. 1556-1598) was the most powerful monarch of his age: he governed from his Escorial palace near Madrid ('the wonder of the world') via a vast bureaucracy of paper memoranda, controlled the silver of Potosí (Bolivia) and Zacatecas (Mexico) that funded European warfare for a century, sent the Armada against Protestant England (1588, defeated by weather and Francis Drake), and fought the Eighty Years' War against Dutch independence simultaneously. The annual silver fleets from the Americas transformed the European economy — inflating prices across Europe (the 'Price Revolution') in history's first global commodity shock.

The dynasty's decline: Philip IV's reign (r. 1621-1665) saw the loss of Portugal (1640), the Catalan Revolt (1640), and a string of military defeats. The 'Spanish Habsburgs' are often cited as a case study in dynastic decline through inbreeding — Charles II ('El Hechizado,' the bewitched), the last Spanish Habsburg (r. 1665-1700), was so physically and cognitively disabled from centuries of consanguineous marriages that he could barely chew; his death without heirs triggered the War of the Spanish Succession (1701-1714) that installed the Bourbon dynasty.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Spanish House of Habsburg — governing history's first truly global empire, funding European warfare with American silver that reshaped the global economy, and shaping Latin American civilization for 300 years — is one of history's most consequential dynasties; their empire's trade connections created the first economically integrated world system.
